# The Many Faces of the Virgin: A Journey Through Sacred Geography

The poem unfolds as an extraordinary pilgrimage, tracing the symbolic passage of "the virgin" across vast and varied geographies—from the tropical islands of the Philippines to the coastal town of Petatlán in Mexico. This is no simple linear journey but rather a transformative odyssey through which she becomes intimately woven into the fabric of the natural and cultural landscapes she traverses. She emerges alongside desert trees standing sentinel in arid expanses, vast seas that connect distant shores, and mountains that anchor the earth to sky. Through this geographic wandering, the virgin becomes less a fixed religious icon and more a living embodiment of place itself, absorbing the character of each landscape she inhabits.

This fluidity of identity is perhaps most striking in the poem's use of layered, often contrasting epithets. She appears as the "virgin of gold filigree," evoking delicate craftsmanship and colonial wealth; then transforms into the "virgin of mud brick ruins," summoning images of ancient civilizations crumbling into dust; and again shifts into the "virgin of mercury," a title heavy with toxic and industrial connotations. These juxtapositions are not accidental but purposeful, suggesting a complex fusion where sacredness intertwines inseparably with material culture and environmental history. She is not merely blessed by these places and substances—she becomes them, absorbing their histories into her very being.

Central to the poem's power is its persistent linkage of the virgin to systems of exploitation and extraction. The imagery draws directly from extractive industries—tin mines that hollowed out mountains, copper deposits that fed distant empires, mercury that poisoned as it purified precious metals. Alongside these mineral references, the poem introduces human cost through images of pearldiving children, their small bodies laboring beneath ocean surfaces for treasures they would never possess. These combined references to mineral and human extraction work together to expose the colonial and economic undertones running beneath the surface of religious veneration, suggesting that devotion and exploitation have long traveled hand in hand through history.

Yet the virgin resists simple categorization as either purely spiritual or purely worldly. The poem positions her simultaneously as a "saint of commonplaces" and a "saint of badlands"—titles that deliberately blur the boundaries between the sacred and the mundane, between glorified spaces and forgotten, marginalized territories. She sanctifies not grand cathedrals alone but the overlooked corners of existence, the barren lands that history often disregards. This duality allows her to exist simultaneously in realms typically kept separate: the holy and the ordinary, the celebrated and the abandoned.

The poem reaches its resolution not through definitive answers but through an embrace of perpetual transformation. She becomes ultimately defined by "naming and renaming," a figure whose identity refuses to calcify into a single, fixed meaning. Rather than serving as a vessel for divination or prophecy—rather than pointing toward some predetermined future—she embodies "goldleafed skin," a surface both precious and provisional, suggesting that her true nature lies not in what she predicts or promises, but in her endless capacity for reinvention across the very geographies and histories that have shaped her.

# The Copper Virgin: A Litany of Passage

## I. Departure

She leaves Manila in the hold of a galleon,
not as passenger but as cargo,
her wooden face wrapped in silk
that once wrapped tea, that once wrapped
the tongues of women who wove
prayers into thread before the friars came
with their own thread, their own weaving
of story onto story until no one
remembers which god wore
which face first.

Call her Nuestra Señora. Call her
nothing her mother would recognize.

## II. The Water Between

Six months at sea and the salt
gets into everything—
into the grain of her carved hands,
into the pearl-shell eyes
some sailor's wife gave her
in place of paint,
into the space where her name
used to sit comfortably
in one mouth, one tongue,
one village's particular grief.

Thorns from a crown no one asked her to wear.
Shells from a shore she never touched.
Jade traded three ports back
for passage, for luck, for the captain's
fever to break before Acapulco.

She collects gods like barnacles.
She collects grief like ballast.

## III. Landfall

Petatlán receives her
the way a wound receives salt—
necessary, unbidden, burning
into something that might
eventually be called healing.

The fishermen who find her
washed up or carried up
or dreamed up (the story changes
depending on who needs her
to have arrived by miracle
versus by trade route)
do not ask if she is tired.

They give her a new dress.
They give her a new name.
They give her their dead
to carry, the way every ocean
gives its dead to whatever
floats.

## IV. The Weight of Metals

Mercury from the mines that killed
the men who might have carved
her first true face—
before Manila, before the friars,
before the word *virgin* meant
anything but *conquered*,
anything but *silent*,
anything but *still*.

She carries copper in her veins now,
extracted, refined, transformed
into something that can be shipped,
something that can be sold,
something that can be worshipped
without ever being asked
what she wanted
to become.

Every empire needs its icons portable.
Every icon becomes, eventually,
a ledger of what was taken
to make her holy.

## V. Syncretism, or the Art of Wearing Other Faces

She is Guadalupe here, Kannon there,
she is the nameless goddess
of a hundred flooded rice terraces,
she is Mary if Mary had survived
the Pacific, if Mary had learned
to breathe underwater,
if Mary had let her skin
turn the color of every coast
that claimed her.

The friars painted her brown
then called the brown miraculous.
The traders carved her small
then called the smallness portable grace.
The believers dressed her heavy
then called the weight devotion.

She never asked for any of this.
She never asked for the crown of thorns
or the crown of shells or the crown
of overlapping histories
pressed like a migraine
into her wooden skull.

## VI. What Endures

But listen—
she is not stone. She is not
the finished thing they wanted,
frozen in one gesture
of eternal, patient grace.

She breathes in the space
between one name and the next.
She remembers Manila
even while she answers
to Petatlán.
She holds the mercury and the jade
and the thorns and the shells
not as decoration
but as evidence—

*I was here. I was traded.
I was renamed. I survived
the renaming.*

Every layer they added
trying to make her theirs
she wears now as testimony,
not to their conquest
but to her own
persistent, inconvenient
pulse.

She is not your icon.
She is your witness.

She was always
watching.

# From Pilipinas to Petatlán: Echoes of an Ancient Maritime Route

The journey from the Philippines (Pilipinas) to Petatlán, a coastal municipality in the Mexican state of Guerrero, traces back to one of history's most significant transoceanic trade routes: the Manila-Acapulco Galleon Trade, which flourished from 1565 to 1815.

## Historical Context

For 250 years, Spanish galleons crossed the Pacific Ocean, connecting the Philippines to Mexico's western coastline. While Acapulco served as the primary port for this trade, the broader Guerrero coast—including areas near Petatlán—was part of this vast network of exchange that linked Asia to the Americas and, eventually, to Europe.

These voyages carried more than just merchandise like silk, spices, porcelain, and precious goods. They facilitated a profound cultural exchange, bringing Filipino sailors, artisans, and even entire communities to Mexican shores. Many settled along the Pacific coast, leaving traces of their heritage in local customs, cuisine, and even linguistic borrowings that persist today.

## Petatlán's Place in This Legacy

Petatlán, though smaller than Acapulco, existed within this larger regional context of Pacific coast communities shaped by centuries of transoceanic contact. The town's name itself derives from the Nahuatl word for "place of petates" (woven mats), reflecting the indigenous heritage that predates Spanish colonization but which later intertwined with influences arriving via the galleon trade.

## A Modern Reflection

Today, the phrase "from Pilipinas to Petatlán" might symbolize more than a historical trade route—it represents the enduring connections between Filipino and Mexican peoples, built on shared colonial history, similar culinary traditions (like the use of coconut, tropical fruits, and certain cooking techniques), and comparable experiences of resilience along vulnerable coastal geographies.

This distant yet meaningful connection reminds us how interconnected our world has been for centuries, long before modern globalization, through the currents of the Pacific Ocean that once carried galleons laden with goods, ideas, and people between these two culturally rich regions.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write an experimental prose poem tracing a Virgin Mary figure's journey from the Philippines to Petatlán, Mexico, blending Catholic iconography with colonial trade history.
counterfactuals.output:
**Cargo of the Immaculate**

*i. Intramuros*

Before she was a mother she was a tusk, and before that, an elephant grazing somewhere the ledgers never name — *marfil, procedencia desconocida* — and the Chinese hands in Parián that hollowed her out worked by candlelight, humming something that was not quite a hymn, shaving the ivory thin as a wafer, thin as something meant to dissolve on a tongue. They gave her a face before they gave her a name. Sangley fingers, Tagalog breath, a rosary of sawdust settling in the humidity like snow that has heard of snow only in scripture.

*Ave, gratia plena* — but plena with what. With tusk-dust. With trade wind. With the smell of copra and camphor already sealing itself into her wrists.

*ii. the hold*

Manifest, June, the galleon *Nuestra Señora del —* (illegible, salt-eaten):

*4 crates ivory saints
12 bales silk, Canton
3 sacks pepper
1 Virgin, disassembled for the crossing, her head packed separate from her hands so that for six months she is only a face floating in straw, praying to no body, or a pair of hands folded around nothing, praying to no face.*

The Pacific does not know the word Pacific. It heaves. Below deck the moths get into the silk and into the gold leaf of her mantle and eat a small constellation into her shoulder, so that she arrives already wounded, already a map of some other hunger.

Sailors pray to her in pieces the way you'd pray to a saint you'd cut in half to share.

*Santa María, tell the compass something. Tell the compass we are still Catholic out here where the water has no diocese.*

*iii. Acapulco, the unwrapping*

Customs opens her like a letter. Someone writes *derechos reales* in a column beside her value, appraised in reales as if grace could be taxed at port, and maybe it can — maybe that's the oldest sacrament, the toll booth at the edge of the miraculous.

They reassemble her on the dock. Head to neck, hand to wrist, a resurrection performed by bored officials with salt-cracked knuckles. The Filipino carver's face is still under her Chinese lacquer is still under the Spanish gold leaf is still under the sun of Guerrero, which has never touched anything so pale and sets about, immediately, to change that.

*iv. the road inland, on the backs of mules, in procession*

They renamed the rivers as they crossed them and she let them, being made of ivory, being made of listening.

Petatlán rises out of the heat like something that has been waiting under a petate, under woven palm, patient as clay. The mule train arrives with her lashed to a litter of cedar, and the villagers do not ask what ocean she crossed. They ask what she is hungry for. This is the first true question anyone has asked her since the elephant.

*v. enshrinement*

They give her a new mantle, this one stitched by hands that have never seen Manila, hands that know instead the particular blue of jacaranda and copal smoke and the going-under of the sun behind the sierra like a host lowered into a mouth.

She keeps the moth-hole. No one repairs it. It becomes, in time, a relic within the relic — *here the sea ate her, here the sea left its signature, here is where three oceans and two empires and one elephant still live under the gold.*

They call her by a new name now, a Guerrero name, a name that tastes of river-silt and copal instead of camphor and Latin. But if you hold her up to the light — if you are permitted, which you are not, which no one is, except the moths, except the customs clerks of 1620, except this poem —

you can still see, faint as a watermark, the tusk.
The elephant.
The Parián candlelight.
The six months she prayed to herself in two unconnected pieces
across a sea that did not yet have her name for God.

*Ora pro nobis,* the manifest says, filed under miscellaneous, filed under cargo, filed under mother.

counterfactuals.prompt: Generate a poem exploring the Manila Galleon trade route through a mythic, devotional lens—focus on imagery of minerals, sea voyages, and religious syncretism, using repetitive "virgin of" phrasing like a rosary litany.
counterfactuals.output:
# Litany of the Silver Route

Virgin of Acapulco, salt-crowned, patient at the pier,
watch the *Nao de China* swallow the horizon,
her hold heavy with your name in a hundred tongues.

Virgin of the Mercury Mines, whose lungs are quicksilver,
whose lace is cinnabar dust settling on Potosí's dead,
pray for the men who feed the mountain and are fed to it.

Virgin of the Manila Rope, twisted from abacá,
you bind the galleon's ribs against the taifun's teeth,
you are the knot that does not confess to breaking.

Virgin of Cebu, small and dark and older than the friars,
they dressed you in Iberian gold and called it conversion,
but the ivory of your face remembers monsoon, not Madrid.

Virgin of the Ledger, keeper of the *situado*,
count the pesos ground from Zacatecas' silver veins,
each coin your rosary bead, each bead a buried Indian.

Virgin of Coral and Camphor, of cloves sealed in wax,
you smell of Molucca, you taste of Canton,
you are traded twelve thousand miles and never asked.

Virgin of the Latitude, hidden in the astrolabe's eye,
guide the pilot through the doldrums' long confession,
the sea gives no absolution, only wind or none.

Virgin of Typhoon Season, veiled in green-black cloud,
how many galleons kneel at your feet unfinished,
their silver scattered like seed on a barren floor of coral?

Virgin of the Syncretic Wound, half Aztec, half Visayan,
they carved you from santol wood and narra wood alike,
your wounds are the wounds of every colonized grain.

Virgin of the Return Voyage, laden now with silk,
with porcelain thin as a martyr's collarbone,
you sail westward bearing what the East could not keep.

Virgin of the Empty Warehouse, after the trade route dies,
when steam replaces sail and silver finds new roads,
what remains of you but incense, myth, and rust?

Virgin of all Crossings, of monsoon and of Mass,
pray for us who melted in your holds—
mineral, spice, and flesh, indistinguishable cargo,
each of us a coin stamped with your quiet face.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

barefoot on ballast stone and coral dust

her hands still full of foreign metal

# Virgin of the Pacific Rim

Virgin of the copper vein, of the mountain
opened like a wound that will not scar,
teach me the geography of what was taken.

Virgin of the tuna boats at dawn,
of the silver churches built from silver mined
by hands that never learned to hold a coin—

Virgin of the atoll, of the coral bleached
to bone-white rosaries, of the tide
that keeps its own liturgy, indifferent to our need—

Virgin of the sugar cane, the missionary's Latin
grafted onto tongues that already had a word
for god, for rain, for the ancestors underground—

Virgin of Manila, of the galleon's hold
stuffed with porcelain and prayer,
of the Pacific as a highway paved with debt—

Virgin of the nickel mine in the rainforest's lung,
of the smoke that rises like an offering
to no one, to the shareholders, to the sky—

Virgin of the pearl diver's collapsed ear,
of the depth that does not care for sainthood,
only pressure, only the long descent—

Virgin of the flag changed six times
on the same stretch of black sand,
of the name that means "found" in someone else's language—

Virgin of the diaspora, praying in a borrowed accent
to a face that might be her own,
might be the volcano's, might be no one's—

Virgin of what floats: the plastic, the passport,
the novena whispered over instant coffee,
the island that keeps rising though the maps forget it—

Teach me this: to be geography and worshipper both,
to be extracted and to remain,
to hold the wound like a rosary, like a shore.
